faq.q: Why is depth of invasion important in staging?

faq.a: Yes, especially HPV‑16 infection in younger patients without traditional risk factors.
faq.q: Can oral SCC arise without tobacco or alcohol use?

faq.a: It describes widespread epithelial changes from carcinogen exposure, predisposing to multiple primary tumours.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with a 3‑cm ulcer on the lateral tongue and a 2‑cm ipsilateral node – what is the TNM stage and immediate management? — T2 (size) with depth >5 mm, N1, M0 → Stage III; plan wide excision with ipsilateral neck dissection.

A 30‑year‑old woman with a non‑healing buccal mucosa ulcer, HIV‑positive, no tobacco use – which aetiologic pathway is most likely and how does it affect prognosis? — HPV‑related pathway; generally better response to radiotherapy and improved survival.

You have no CT scanner; how do you assess nodal disease before surgery? — Perform high‑resolution neck ultrasound with fine‑needle aspiration of suspicious nodes; if unavailable, base decision on clinical examination and consider elective neck dissection.
During surgery you encounter mandibular bone invasion – what change in management is required? — Extend resection to include segmental mandibulectomy and plan postoperative radiotherapy.
A patient develops severe mucositis after chemoradiotherapy – which supportive measure is essential? — Aggressive oral care, analgesia, and nutritional support (enteral feeding if needed).

Why is cisplatin preferred over methotrexate in concurrent chemoradiotherapy for oral SCC? — Cisplatin radiosensitises tumour cells with proven survival benefit; methotrexate has higher toxicity and less evidence in this setting.

A biopsy shows well‑differentiated SCC but the patient has a 1‑cm lesion – is a neck dissection still indicated? — Yes, because depth of invasion may be >5 mm and occult nodal disease is common; elective neck dissection is recommended.
What preventive advice would you give a community with high khat chewing rates? — Counsel on reducing khat and tobacco co‑use, improve oral hygiene, and promote regular oral examinations.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Oral SCC is the predominant oral cancer, driven by tobacco/alcohol or HPV pathways and characterised by field cancerisation. Early recognition, appropriate staging and multidisciplinary management are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Biopsy must include depth of invasion
Report includes grade, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion
sections.p: A malignant neoplasm of the oral mucosal epithelium, most often arising as a keratinising squamous cell carcinoma. Diagnosis requires a tissue biopsy with histopathology confirming invasive SCC.

b: T1 ≤2 cm and ≤5 mm depth; T2 ≤2 cm and >5 mm or 2–4 cm ≤10 mm depth; etc.
N0 = no clinical/radiologic nodal disease; N1 = single ipsilateral node ≤3 cm
sections.p: Staged using the AJCC 8th edition TNM system, which incorporates tumour size, depth of invasion, nodal involvement, and distant metastasis.

b: Chewing khat or betel quid with tobacco increases risk
Chronic oral ulceration from poor dentition or herbal irritants
Immunosuppression (HIV) amplifies HPV‑related risk
sections.p: Two dominant aetiologic pathways dominate in East Africa: (1) tobacco (smoked or smokeless) and alcohol use causing TP53 mutations; (2) high‑risk HPV‑16 infection with p16 over‑expression, often in younger, non‑smokers.

b: Persistent ulcer >2 weeks
Firm, indurated margins
Occult neck node in 30‑40 % at presentation
sections.p: Patients usually notice a non‑healing ulcer or exophytic mass on the tongue, floor of mouth, or buccal mucosa, often with induration, pain, or dysphagia.
Focused investigations confirm diagnosis, assess extent and guide treatment.

t.b: Confirms malignant histology and grade; essential before any therapy

t.a: Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of head and neck
t.b: Answers tumour size, depth, bone invasion, and nodal status; if unavailable, ultrasound of neck can assess nodes
Screens for distant lung metastasis; if normal, no further thoracic imaging needed
Identifies immunosuppression that may affect prognosis and treatment choice
Distinguishes HPV‑related SCC, which has a better prognosis and may influence radiotherapy planning

b: Airway compromise from tongue base tumour
Bleeding from ulcerated lesion
Mandibular invasion causing pathological fracture
sections.p: Rapid growth, airway obstruction, severe pain, or sudden neck swelling demand urgent assessment.

b: Wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins; neck dissection if N+
Concurrent cisplatin‑based chemoradiotherapy for stage III/IV or unresectable tumours
Analgesia, nutritional support (NG tube or gastrostomy), oral hygiene
Avoid methotrexate in renal impairment; avoid bleomycin in pulmonary disease
sections.p: Multidisciplinary care: surgery for resectable disease, radiotherapy ± chemotherapy for advanced cases, and supportive measures.

b: Clinical review every 3 months for 2 years, then 6 monthly
Educate on self‑exam of oral cavity
Counselling on tobacco/khaini cessation; consider community HPV vaccination
sections.p: Regular surveillance for recurrence and second primary tumours; primary prevention focuses on tobacco cessation and HPV vaccination where feasible.

Epulis or pyogenic granuloma
